opus-5.5.text:
Part of it is that a lot of the hardest open problems in alignment are, underneath, questions about what a weaker party can reliably verify about a stronger one. If you have a system that's more capable than you in some domain, how do you check that what it's telling you is true, or that it's behaving the way you intended? That's very close to questions complexity theorists have thought hard about for decades: interactive proofs, verifier–prover setups, what a polynomial-time checker can be convinced of by an all-powerful prover. Debate as an alignment proposal came directly out of that analogy.

The analogy only gets you so far, though. Theory tells you what's possible in principle under clean assumptions. Real models are messy, humans make systematic errors, and the honest strategy may be computationally harder than the dishonest one. So you need people who can take a complexity-theoretic idea and ask whether it survives contact with real training dynamics, real human judges, and real failure modes. You also want people from learning theory, cryptography, cognitive science, and the experimental ML side.

Putting these fields together matters because each one alone tends to stall in a predictable way. Theorists can produce elegant results that don't touch the actual bottleneck. Empiricists can run lots of experiments without a framework that says which results would change our minds. When they work closely together, the theory points to the experiments that matter, and the experiments show which assumptions are load-bearing and which are fake. I think that loop is how we get from "this seems like a promising idea" to "we have reasons to trust this protocol at scale."

There's also a talent argument. There are many very strong people in theoretical computer science and adjacent areas who'd find these problems fascinating but have never been given a clean statement of them. A lot of the work is translation: turning vague worries about superhuman systems into crisp open problems a mathematician can work on. If we do that well, I think we can draw on a much larger pool of researchers than alignment has had so far.

r001.rationale: It describes alignment as checking what a weaker party can verify about a stronger system, connecting this to complexity theory’s verifier–prover models and polynomial-time checkers.

r002.rationale: It argues that theory needs to be tested against real-world behavior and that theory and experiments together can reveal which assumptions hold, supporting a more rigorous understanding of alignment.

r003.rationale: It says fields can make progress by working closely together, but does not identify economies of scale from sharing research resources as the mechanism.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that alignment has, for most of its life, been a field where people argue about intuitions, and the thing that makes a field actually move is when you can turn intuitions into statements that are either true or false. Complexity theory is one of the best tools we have for doing that.

Take the basic problem we care about. You've got a system that is, in some domain, much more capable than you are, and you want to be able to trust what it tells you. Stated that way it sounds hopeless. But complexity theorists have been studying exactly that shape of problem for forty years. The whole framework of interactive proofs is about a weak verifier with limited resources checking claims from a powerful, possibly dishonest prover. That's not a loose analogy. It's structurally the same question, and there are real theorems about when it works and when it doesn't.

So one thing that happens when you bring those people into the room is that they immediately start asking the right annoying questions. If I say "we'll have two models debate and a human judges the outcome," a complexity theorist will say: what's the judge allowed to do, how many rounds, what's the honest strategy, what's the assumption on the judge that makes honesty win? And when you try to answer those questions you find out that some of your proposals fall apart and some of them become much sharper. The debate work I was involved in went through exactly that. The early versions had a lot of hand-waving. The later versions have actual protocols where you can say, under these assumptions about the judge, the honest player has a winning strategy, and you can also see where the assumptions bite. That's progress of a kind you can't get from running more experiments.

The second reason is more about the division of labour. There's a tendency in machine learning to think every question should be settled empirically, and empirical work is essential, I'm not knocking it. But a lot of the questions in alignment are about systems we don't have yet, operating in regimes we can't test. Theory is how you reason about things you can't run. And the specific kind of theory that's useful here is not deep learning theory about convergence rates. It's the kind that models adversaries and asks what guarantees survive when the other party is trying to fool you. Cryptographers and complexity theorists have the right instincts for that almost by reflex.

And then the third thing, honestly, is that putting people in the same building matters more than it should. A complexity theorist on their own will prove beautiful results about an idealised prover and verifier that have nothing to do with how a language model actually fails. An ML researcher on their own will build something that works until it doesn't and not know why. The useful work happens at the boundary, where someone says "that assumption about the verifier is unrealistic, here's what the human actually does" and someone else says "okay, then here's a different protocol, and here's the obstruction if you weaken it further." You get that iteration maybe weekly if people share coffee. You get it maybe yearly if they share a conference.

I should be honest that the theory doesn't hand you a safe system. It hands you a clear picture of what you'd need to be true for a system to be safe, and that's a different thing. But I'd much rather be in a world where we know precisely which assumptions we're leaning on than one where we're hoping and calling it a plan.

r001.rationale: It describes a limited-resource verifier evaluating claims from a much more powerful prover and identifies this as structurally relevant to alignment.

r002.rationale: It argues alignment should move from intuition to claims that can be tested or proved, and connects that need to combining theory and empirical machine learning.

r003.rationale: It says co-location enables more frequent collaboration, but does not identify economies of scale from shared research resources as a reason progress could accelerate.

astra-6.text:
I think alignment has questions at its core that are very close to questions people have studied in other fields, but the connections haven’t been fully worked through. Complexity theory, for example, asks about the difference between solving a problem and checking a solution. That seems directly relevant if we’re trying to supervise a system that can do things we can’t do ourselves.

The hope is that even if a model is much better than us at finding an answer, there might be a way for it to present the answer—or for another model to challenge it—that lets us reliably judge what’s going on. But that’s a conditional hope. We need to understand what assumptions make it work, where it fails, and whether those assumptions survive contact with actual machine learning systems.

Bringing people together at Resolution could help because those questions need both kinds of expertise. Someone from complexity theory might recognise a useful mathematical structure, while someone working on alignment can explain why the clean formulation leaves out the difficult part. That back-and-forth can give us better questions as well as better answers. I wouldn’t expect a theorem to solve alignment on its own, but I do think it can help us distinguish a promising approach from one that only looks promising because we haven’t made the problem precise.

r001.rationale: The response discusses models outperforming humans and the difference between solving and checking problems, but does not identify complexity theory’s ability to model relationships between weaker and stronger amounts of computation.

r002.rationale: It says alignment questions need to be worked through, their assumptions tested, and the problem made precise, and explains that bringing complexity and alignment expertise together can help do that.

r003.rationale: The response gives a rationale based on combining expertise and exchanging ideas, but does not mention economies of scale from shared research resources.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is that alignment has questions which look very different depending on which field you come from. If you ask, “How can a person supervise a system that understands something much better than they do?”, that sounds like an AI problem. But it’s also a question about verification: how much easier is it to check an answer than to produce it? And what kinds of interaction make checking possible? Those are questions complexity theory gives us tools to think about.

That doesn’t mean you can take a theorem and immediately turn it into a practical alignment method. The assumptions matter enormously. A protocol might work if a verifier can reliably check some small piece of an argument, and then the practical question is whether humans, perhaps assisted by models, can actually do that.

What I’d like at Resolution is a tight feedback loop between those perspectives. The theory helps us identify what a method needs in order to work, experiments tell us which assumptions fail, and that sends us back to a better theoretical question. Having people who can really challenge each other’s assumptions could make that loop much faster.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a stronger system with a human supervisor and says complexity theory can help analyze verification, but it does not clearly identify modeling relationships between weaker and stronger amounts of computation.

r002.rationale: It describes using theory and experiments to refine alignment questions, but does not present a need for a more rigorous understanding of AI alignment as a general reason to draw on multiple fields.

r003.rationale: It says cross-field interaction could speed a theory–experiment feedback loop, but does not mention economies of scale or shared research resources.
